Posted March 24, 2003
Analysis By Richard Cowan

Remember the name, Marco Cappato.

In late January of last year, I went to Stockport, England, to visit the now closed Dutch Experience, the UK's first cannabis café.

While I was there I watched as Marco Panella, the venerable leader of the Transnational Radical Party, and a Member of the European Parliament, tried to get arrested with a small quantity of cannabis at the Stockport police station. The police seized the cannabis, but refused to arrest Panella.

Panella's actions were in support of two of his fellow MEPs, Chris Davies, the local MEP and Marco Cappato, of Milan, who is another Italian MEP. They, in turn, had gotten themselves arrested in December of 2001 in support of Colin Davies (no kin to Chris), the co-founder of the Dutch Experience, along with Nol van Schaik.
See
The War On the Sick, Dying and Disabled by the Media/Police State Complex: Colin Davies Sentenced to Three Years. Fifty Armed Police Close The Dutch Experience (Again). Arrest Colin's Brother.

In December, 2001, Cappato had spent the night in the Stockport jail, because after being arrested on camera and getting the arresting officer to repeat everything he refused bail when he was booked.

He had returned to Stockport with Panella. (I had met Cappato briefly in 1993 at an anti-prohibitionist conference in Rome, and to my surprise, nine years later, he actually remembered me, an invaluable skill for a politician.)

Now a year later, Greater Manchester police said Cappato was charged because he refused to accept a caution, which is what the UK calls its intermediate version of decrim and jailed because he refused to sign the bail sheet. Idiotically, the police had used 12 officers to arrest him, and then had the audacity to complain that he had wasted their time.

In fact, he had refused to pay the US$160 fine, even though he had paid the US$3,500 court costs. (The UK pound is around US$1.60)

Cappato, who is still only 32, is obviously a stand-up sort of guy, but also I am convinced that he, Panella, and Davies really get it. Although they are not cannabis activists per se, they clearly understand the nature of cannabis prohibition, and take it very seriously.

Unfortunately, the UK establishment does not. Later this year, the UK will formally implement its phony decriminalization, and probably increase penalties for growing and selling.
See
Bonkers in Britain: New Cannabis Rules Please No One, Confuse Everyone. Watching the Political Establishment Make Fools of Themselves. Analysis by Richard Cowan

Cappato told the Associated Press, " This was a civil disobedience action in support of others. I submitted myself to the consequences of the law to help push forward public opinion in Britain, where drug laws are in breach of international conventions on drugs. Unfortunately, nobody noticed because of the war. "

No, alas, we cannot really blame the war.

If this had been something that the media considers important, such as Michael Jackson's nose, it would have been reported. The sad fact is that even the anti-prohibitionist UK media, which includes most of the quality broadsheet newspapers, such as the Telegraph, the Guardian, and the Independent, have ignored Colin Davies ordeal. They simply refuse to take the issue seriously.
See
De Facto Cannabis Decriminalization In Scotland? Is Crack Epidemic In Brixton the Fault of Cannabis Decriminalization? Or Is The UK Drugs Problem Just Part of Crises In Law Enforcement and Journalism?

The fact is that there is a terrible tendency toward selective sensitivity in the media, and not just in the UK. Too often it seems that both those who are for and against the war in Iraq are more sensitive to the rights and/or suffering of the Iraqis than of their own people in their own jails. But it's only cannabis.
See
Is the War On Drugs A Just War. "? Should It Be Easier To Justify Violence Against A Foreign Dictatorship Than Against Peaceful Citizens Of One's Own Country?

No, it's only freedom.

So remember Marco Cappato. He knows what's important.
